title: Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer of Commonwealth Edison Company re the 07/24/2026 tariff filing under ER26-3257.

UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                 BEFORE THE
                   FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                                                  )
Commonwealth Edison Company                       )         Docket No. ER26-3257-000
                                                  )

                 MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER AND ANSWER OF
                      COMMONWEALTH EDISON COMPANY

       PowerHouse Hillwood Holding LLC (“Hillwood”) has told a federal court its Project is

“sunk” and only a (meritless) damages claim remains.1 That is reason enough to cancel the

Transmission Security Agreement (“TSA”). Yet seven business days ahead of the Commission’s

deadline to act on Commonwealth Edison Company’s (“ComEd”) Notice of Cancellation

(“Notice”), Hillwood filed a 74-page Answer seeking to avoid that result.2 Given that Hillwood

has no project and no need for a TSA, Hillwood’s goal is transparent: to create confusion and delay

cancellation, which Hillwood apparently thinks will bolster its new claims for “money damages.”3

       Hillwood’s lengthy Answer changes nothing. In Part A, we update the Commission on

Hillwood’s pivot to damages in federal court. In Part B, we show that Hillwood’s Answer leaves

unobstructed the Commission’s path to accept the Notice on either of ComEd’s two independent

grounds. First, Hillwood has no project and no active Retail Service Application (“Retail

Application”), and the Commission routinely cancels contracts when the associated projects fail.

Second, Hillwood still has no valid argument for its $1 letter-of-credit posting. Finally, we respond

briefly to Hillwood’s grab bag of arguments that the Commission can resolve easily.

1
  PowerHouse Hillwood Holding LLC v. Commonwealth Edison Co., No. 1:26-cv-8860, Dkt. 92, Transcript
of Proceedings at 47:23-48:1 (N.D. Ill. Aug. 28, 2026) (the “Federal Court Case” and “August 28 Tr.”).
2
  Commonwealth Edison Co., Docket No. ER26-3257, Answer in Opposition of PowerHouse Hillwood
Holding LLC to Commonwealth Edison Motion for Leave to Answer, or in the Alternative, Answer and
Request to File Answer of PowerHouse Hillwood Holding LLC (Sept. 11, 2026) (“Hillwood Answer”).
3

Preliminary Injunction at 1 (N.D. Ill. Aug. 31, 2026) (“Withdrawal Motion”).
 I.      ANSWER

        A.       Hillwood No Longer Seeks Judicial Relief To Advance Its Project And Is Only
                 Pursuing Damages.

        Hillwood’s Answer is inconsistent with what it told the federal court: It has no viable data

center project and is now only seeking damages.4 On August 26, 2026, after the Court decided to

stay the Federal Court Case in favor of the Commission’s primary jurisdiction,5 Hillwood sought

emergency judicial relief (in part) to stop ComEd from cancelling a long-lead equipment contract

based on Hillwood’s failure to pay deposits required by ComEd’s retail tariff.6 Hillwood told the

court that the “viability of the Project hangs in the balance”; that “[a]bsent injunctive relief, by the

time FERC acts, no Project may be left”7; and that without an injunction “we are sunk.”8

        The Court, however, made clear no such relief would be forthcoming, observing that

“anything involving the [Retail Application] has to go before the” Illinois Commerce Commission

(“ICC”) and that the Court had not “seen where Hillwood has filed anything before the ICC . . . .”9

Hillwood then withdrew the motion and informed the Court that it “regrettably concluded that the

most appropriate remedy . . . is to pursue money damages rather than injunctive relief.”10

figure out how to post some sort of security . . . .”).

         B.      ComEd’s Two Independent Grounds For Cancellation Are Straightforward,
                Largely Undisputed, And Legally Supportable.

        ComEd’s Notice seeks cancellation on two independent bases: (1) the (still) undisputed

fact that ComEd terminated Hillwood’s Retail Application on July 24; and (2) Hillwood’s refusal

to comply with the TSA’s Letter of Credit requirement by posting $1. Despite Hillwood’s efforts

to complicate matters, nothing in the Hillwood Answer undermines either ground.

                1.       Hillwood Has No Answer To The Termination Of Its Retail Application
                         And The End Of The Project.

        Cancelling the TSA is just and reasonable because the underlying Project and Retail

Application are no more. Hillwood does not dispute ComEd’s showing that the Commission

routinely accepts cancellation of jurisdictional agreements when, as here, the agreement exists to

facilitate a project that has failed11—including other similarly situated ComEd transmission

security agreements.12 The dispositive question, then, is: Is there a project taking retail service for

the TSA to support? As ComEd explained fully,13 the answer is no, for two independent reasons.

        First, no project exists. Hillwood’s Answer suggests the Project remains alive and vaguely

gestures at “injunctive relief” courts can provide.14 But as explained, Hillwood withdrew its actual

request for injunctive relief—the one it said was essential for the Project to survive. It also

(“no longer appropriate” to maintain the tariff for deactivated units); PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 195

 withdrew its request for emergency relief from the Commission.15 ComEd then took the steps that

Hillwood sought to enjoin, including cancelling a long-lead contract and moving forward with

planning processes excluding Hillwood.

        Second, Hillwood has no active Retail Application. ComEd’s tariff provides that ComEd

“continues to provide electric service to a retail customer only if all applicable requirements in

these General Terms and Conditions are met and maintained . . . .”16 On July 24, 2026, ComEd

notified Hillwood that “effective immediately, ComEd is terminating the” Retail Application.17

While Hillwood disputes the propriety of that termination,18 it does not dispute that (a) the

termination took effect, (b) any challenge to the termination’s validity “must be determined under

the ComEd retail tariff by arbiters like the ICC,”19 and (c) it has not sought relief from the ICC—

not in the 52 days since the July 24 termination and not in the four months since ComEd requested

additional security under its retail tariff.20 Nor would it matter if Hillwood did so before

September 22. Unlike a Section 205 cancellation notice, the Retail Application’s termination was

immediately effective and remains so unless and until the ICC says otherwise.21 As ComEd’s

Answer explains, with the Retail Application terminated, the TSA should not remain effective.22

                 2.      TSA Letter-of-Credit Issues.

        Although the Commission need not reach these issues to permit ComEd’s cancellation to

take effect, Hillwood’s arguments fail.

        Primary Jurisdiction. Flip-flopping from its August 14, 2026 protest, Hillwood now

insists that the Commission should not decide whether the TSA permitted Hillwood to leave

ComEd and its customers at risk by posting a $1 letter of credit until after commercial operation.

But Hillwood’s new Arkla argument ignores that the federal court already deferred to the

Commission’s primary jurisdiction on these very issues.23 The Court did not reserve any part of

the dispute for judicial determination.24 The Commission should reject Hillwood’s attempt to get

a different answer from a different forum.

        Moreover, for two reasons, Hillwood asks the wrong question and, thus, reaches the wrong

answer.25 First, Hillwood frames the issue as whether the Commission should adjudicate a private

contract dispute. But the issue is whether to accept a notice of cancellation filed under Section

205—a question only the Commission can decide. If the Commission does not accept the

cancellation based on ComEd’s termination of the Retail Application, then whether Hillwood’s $1

letter breached the TSA is not a collateral matter the Commission may leave to others; it is the

predicate for the Section 205 determination before it.              The Commission cannot “decline

jurisdiction” over that question without declining to perform its own statutory function.26




23
   Federal Court Case, Dkt. 53, Minute Order (N.D. Ill. Aug. 20, 2026).
24
   Id.
25
   Hillwood Answer at 20-33; see ComEd Answer at 30 & n.151.

Commission is obliged to assure that the rates . . . are just and reasonable . . . .”).

         Second, the Arkla factors are easily met for the reasons that ComEd explained in its

Answer.27 Hillwood’s primary counter is a 31-year-old Portland General Electric Company

(“PGE”) order that is far off point.28 For starters, PGE involved a request for a declaratory order

about an issue within the Commission’s and courts’ concurrent jurisdiction;29 it was not a

cancellation notice filed under Section 205 within the Commission’s exclusive jurisdiction. The

contract questions there, too, were very different. PGE pertained to interpreting run-of-the-mill

termination provisions that the Commission decided it had no special expertise over, would not

affect other contracts, and did not implicate any special regulatory responsibilities.30 As ComEd

explained, the opposite is true here, and this case is similar to the scores of Commission decisions

issued this century exercising jurisdiction over contract disputes.31

        Merits. Hillwood’s reading of the TSA would leave ComEd and its customers unsecured

for years, including until after the transmission facilities needed to serve Hillwood would have

been planned and built, and after the date by which, on Hillwood’s schedule, the Project would

have been operating.32 The text does not support that result. Section 9(A)(a) required a Letter of

“petition for declaratory order”).

Montana itself had filed a breach of contract lawsuit a week before filing the notice of cancellation with the
Commission. Id. at 62,205, 62,207. The Commission reasonably decided to wait to see how the court
would handle PPL Montana’s own lawsuit on the same issue before resolving its cancellation notice. Id. at
62,207-08. By contrast, here, Hillwood was the party that filed suit, and the Court resolving that suit has
already decided to defer the contract questions to the Commission’s primary jurisdiction.

 Credit no later than a defined number of days after the Effective Date, and Exhibit C provides that

“[u]pon issuance” the letter “shall have a face amount equal to the Credit Support Schedule.”33

       ComEd has laid out its textual arguments and need not rehash them,34 but Hillwood’s

barrage of textual arguments also leaves unanswered two critical practical points. First, the TSA

made Hillwood liable for the Early Termination Fee from the Effective Date forward, including

tens of millions of dollars for the first 180 days, escalating thereafter to hundreds of millions of

dollars. The Letter of Credit secures that fee.35 Hillwood’s reading leaves the fee unsecured

throughout its escalation. Hillwood’s Answer does not mention the fee schedule, the liability from

the start, or the insolvency risk ComEd identified.

       Second, if Hillwood need post only $1 until after the Project reaches commercial operation,

ComEd and its customers have no assurance that any bank will issue the full letter worth hundreds

of millions of dollars when the time comes, even though ComEd would by then have completed

the work needed to bring the data center online.36 Hillwood’s only response is that issuing a $1

letter “establishes a qualifying LC Issuing Bank.”37 But a bank willing to stand behind one dollar

has made no commitment to stand behind hundreds of millions.

       Contract interpretation favors interpretations that are “fair, customary, and such as prudent

persons would naturally execute,”38 and Hillwood does not explain why sophisticated parties

would agree to—or the Commission would accept—a security agreement that so egregiously fails

to provide security. Hillwood’s reading would also create the type of serious harm to ratepayers

responsibility to prevent, by undermining the assurances intended to protect customers from

Hillwood’s default risk.39

       Termination Provision. ComEd’s August 31 Answer explained that if the Commission

agrees Hillwood breached the Letter of Credit requirement, that breach supports cancellation under

Section 205, and nothing in the TSA’s termination provisions forecloses it.40 Hillwood’s response

reduces to the claim that however egregious its breach, the TSA must remain in force until

Hillwood says so—that “every” termination is “conditioned on [its] irrevocable withdrawal of its

retail service application.”41 Nothing in the termination provision supports that bizarre claim.

       Hillwood’s new argument relies on Section 6(B) of the TSA, which if anything cuts against

it. Section 6(B) states that termination and recovery of the Early Termination Fee are ComEd’s

“sole remedies for Customer failure to fulfill any of its obligations set forth in the preceding

sentence.”42 But to begin, Hillwood’s relevant obligations—to provide a letter of credit and fulfill

its retail obligations—are not set forth “in the preceding sentence”; they are addressed elsewhere.

That sentence instead addresses other potential failures, like “timely construct[ing] its New

Customer Facilities.”43 It thus does not limit ComEd’s remedies for the Letter of Credit breach.

Moreover, Hillwood has failed to meet the obligations that Section 6(B) does address: By its own

account, it will not “timely construct” the facilities or reach commercial operation on schedule44

and only seeks damages in court. For those failures, Section 6(B) itself provides that ComEd’s

by Hillwood’s own account, ComEd can terminate the TSA.

               3.      The Remainder Of Hillwood’s Filing Is Meritless.

       ComEd’s Answer. There is no merit to Hillwood’s challenge to ComEd’s motion for leave

to file its August 31 Answer. ComEd filed its Notice on July 24, a routine submission that

complied with the Commission’s requirements and was consistent with notices of cancellation it

has filed for other TSAs.45 Unlike other similarly situated developers, Hillwood decided to litigate

the Notice rather than accept it, filing 71 pages of arguments and evidence.46 ComEd provided a

fulsome Answer addressing Hillwood’s arguments.              That naturally would “assist[] [the

Commission] in [its] decision-making process.”47

       Effective Date. Hillwood’s primary argument in resisting ComEd’s requested effective

date of July 25, 2026—the day after ComEd terminated the Retail Application—is that the TSA

does not prescribe a particular cancellation date when project-ending events or material breaches

occur.48 But as described above, while the TSA may not have a date certain for cancellation,

cancellation is required when the Retail Application is terminated and no project will go forward.

That occurred by July 25. And even if Central Hudson were not squarely applicable (it is),49 the

legal rule is that the Commission can grant an earlier effective date when it finds good cause. The

 Commission can easily find good cause under these circumstances, where the effective date aligns

with the terminations of the conditions precedent for a project to proceed.

        Suspension/Hearing. No suspension or hearing is required. The only disputed facts that

Hillwood can find are the factual predicates underlying ComEd’s termination of the Retail

Application.50 Those issues—as Hillwood’s Answer concedes51—would be for the ICC to decide.

The only facts the Commission need find on the termination of the Retail Application are that:

(1) ComEd terminated the Retail Application on July 24, 2026; and (2) no tribunal with

jurisdiction over that issue has rendered that termination ineffective. Those facts are undisputed,

and again, Hillwood has not even sought relief from the ICC. Nor will anything happen in federal

court that will bear on the Commission’s decision-making during the suspension period Hillwood

seeks. Now that Hillwood has converted its federal suit into a damages case, no resolution is likely

forthcoming in that period. The Commission also should not ignore Hillwood’s admitted goal—

to extract a settlement from ComEd, in pursuit of a damages claim concerning a dead project.52

That is not what the Commission’s suspension and hearing procedures are for.

        Other Retail Issues. Hillwood devotes pages to an ICC-ordered audit of ComEd’s

administration of Rider NS.53 The audit is a distraction, for two reasons. First, it concerns a rider

that does not govern Hillwood’s service or the dispute. The tariff provisions at issue—the

requirements to provide a long-lead deposit “as determined by the Company” and to provide land

rights ComEd “reasonably deems necessary”—appear in the General Terms and Conditions.54

Second, the audit confirms ComEd’s point about forum. The ICC ordered it because oversight of

II.     MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER

        ComEd respectfully requests that the Commission accept this answer to address Hillwood’s

74-page submission and assist the Commission in its decision-making process.56

III.    CONCLUSION

        For the foregoing reasons and those stated in ComEd’s Answer, the Commission should

accept ComEd’s cancellation of the TSA, effective July 25, 2026, without a hearing.
